chapter_theme: Paripadal thirattu 2, the Vaiyai fragment: the rain-fed flood reaches Koodal, the whole city rides out to the ford, lovers quarrel over garlands the water carries, the priests refuse the stained river, the bathing at the royal ford of Tirumarutham, and Maran in the flood likened to Indra in the river of the sky.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the river and the town that goes out to meet its flood

paripadal:thirattu:2:1-10.reading: When heavy rain has poured from the lovely sky so that the wide land vanishes, the Vaiyai comes down gathering many fragrant flowers from the tall gem-bright hill of Naagam to Koodal; the town, glad that the river has put on its ornament of water, puts on garlands and every finery, each person outdoing the next, and the market is filled with wares of every colour.
paripadal:thirattu:2:1-10.nuance: The word அணி (ornament) rings through lines 5 to 10: the river is adorned with water, the people with garlands, the town with its dress, the market with goods, so river and city dress for each other before anyone bathes. Line 4 reads சுடுகின்றே, which gives no sense; சூடுகின்றே (Koodal wears the Vaiyai like a garland) fits the line of ornament imagery but is a correction.

thinai_evidence.note: the whole city, king included, going out to the ford: festival praise, not a love situation

paripadal:thirattu:2:11-27.reading: Women soft as tender shoots ride out on decked elephants, with garlands in their hands, wreaths, fine scent, dress, oiled hair and tied locks; others go beside prancing horses or harness carts and chariots, wrap themselves against the heat, make up their quarrels, dance, sing, shout, laugh, run and tire and search for their own people, until no one is left wandering in the town: the learned and the unlearned, the base, parents, wives who never fail their husbands, the king of the golden chariot and gold-walled Koodal itself crowd the Vaiyai's ford.
paripadal:thirattu:2:11-27.nuance: The list in lines 24 to 27 deliberately levels the city: learning and its lack, the low and the chaste, the king and the walls themselves, all end at one ford, and line 23 says that nobody stays behind. Lines 18 and 19 are hard to construe in our text; the reading of them as people wrapping against the heat is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman finds her lover's garland in a rival's hair and demands it: the marutham quarrel

comparisons.tenor: the lovers' shoulders bearing up those who bathe

paripadal:thirattu:2:28-45.reading: At the ford where lovers bathe with each other's shoulders for rafts, the crescent-browed women, not seeing who bathes in secret, each take whatever happens before them to be about themselves; one, seeing the flood carry the fragrant garland from her lover's chest into a stranger's hair, cries 'give it, give it', and the other answers that the flood itself turned and set it there: why should she grieve at what fell out, would such a chance come twice, the river joined it knowingly, what a wonder; and the weeping woman is told that the rival's young breasts and the water serve the other's embrace, and that her own tears serve it too.
paripadal:thirattu:2:28-45.nuance: The rival's defence makes the flood an accomplice that 'knew' what it was doing (அறிந்து புனல் புணர்த்தது), so the festival river replaces the go-between of the akam poems. The last lines turn on the wife: her tears, like the water, only help the other woman, a hard comfort that tells her weeping is a loss in the quarrel. The speakers are not named and line 41 (கயத் தகக) is corrupt, so the division of voices is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a garland worn openly from the flood brings sulking and the town's gossip

paripadal:thirattu:2:46-57.reading: In the Pandya's unbowed Koodal the wives who guard virtue, gem-fair, dark-bodied, pearl-smiling and coral-lipped, play without pause in the Vaiyai's flood with their own jewelled husbands; and one woman, saying that a garland drifting down the flood came to her hair-knot by the turn of fate, takes it and wears it plainly for the land to see, with a heat that wounds the hearts of those who love; before the lovers meet the sulk grows cruel, and once they meet will she not sulk? The gossip of the town comes and spreads.
paripadal:thirattu:2:46-57.nuance: The unit sets two kinds of women in one flood: the wives who guard aram and bathe with their own husbands, and the woman who wears a floating garland as fate's gift so that everyone may see it. The open wearing is the point: what the river delivers by chance becomes a public sign, and the town's அலர் follows. Lines 51 to 56 are knotted in our text and the reading of who sulks is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmins' abstention and the flood's overflow, described as festival scene

paripadal:thirattu:2:58-71.reading: Saying that the river has taken in brewed toddy that bees swarm over, the brahmins give up their dip; saying that it carries the wedding scents young men and women have scattered, the anthanar will not bathe; saying that the Vaiyai is slimy with honey, the aiyar will not even rinse their mouths; and the flood, rushing, roaring, breaking the banks and pouring down, piles foam in rows between bank, hill and sea, spills over every sluice and rolls on to the sea, overflowing every dam.
paripadal:thirattu:2:58-71.nuance: Three names for the priestly class (பார்ப்பார், அந்தணர், ஐயர்) each refuse for a different stain, toddy, lovers' scent and honey, and each stain is a sign of the festival the rest of the town is enjoying: what bars the priest is what makes the river a feast. Lines 64 to 71 stack verbs and nouns without connectives so that the sound runs like the water; the short lines 65, 67, 69 and 71 are probably the half-lines the source leaves unnumbered.

thinai_evidence.note: the bathing at the royal ford is told as sulking and reunion again and again

paripadal:thirattu:2:72-87.reading: On jewelled elephants tall as many hills, young men and women gather in rows and go together to the front ford of Tirumarutham of the king of the gem-hung elephants and chariots, where bards with tight-strung lutes sing the chosen marutham mode; singing and singing, bathing and bathing in the leaping flood, sulking and sulking, longing to be won back, uniting again and again, glad and glad, searching and searching, worn and worn, wearing flowers and bowing again and again, the good women and men bathe in the full Vaiyai until it seems to roar, and the water, the poet tells the worthies of the east, has been wholly used, left like leavings.
paripadal:thirattu:2:72-87.nuance: Lines 78 to 83 double every verb (பாடிப் பாடி, ஆடி ஆடி, ஊடி ஊடி, கூடிக் கூடி) so the cycle of sulking and reunion becomes the rhythm of the bathing itself, sung to the marutham mode that belongs to that quarrel. Lines 84 to 87 are obscure: மழுபொடு is not a word we can fix, and the address குணக்குச் சான்றீர் and the close on leavings (மிச்சிலா) are read tentatively.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the Pandya bathing with his people, likened to Indra

comparisons.tenor: Maran bathing in the Vaiyai with the people of Koodal

paripadal:thirattu:2:88-101.reading: Apart from sandal paste, fragrant garlands, wreaths, scented powder and the flowers slipped from women's hair and men's locks, the water of this Vaiyai shows no colour of its own: it is not clean water but the run-off, cloudy with saffron and bath paste, of those who rinse their mouths at the rain-filled tank and bathe; and when one weighs how Maran of the swelling shoulders and the dreaded killing elephants bathed in the coming flood with the fierce people of Koodal, what is holding the sea-girt world beside it? it is like Indra of the thousand eyes bathing in the river of the high sky.
paripadal:thirattu:2:88-101.nuance: The closing praise turns the impurity the priests shunned (lines 58 to 63) into glory: the river has no colour but the town's ornaments, and the king bathing in that very water is likened to Indra in the heavenly river. Lines 98 and 99 (இரு முந்நீர் வையம் பிடித்து என்னை? யான் ஊர்க்கு ஒரு நிலையும் ஆற்ற இயையா) are uncertain; they may mean that ruling the whole world is nothing beside this bathing, or that the speaker cannot match the sight with any state of the town.

links.note: Kalittokai 98 has the husband excuse his absence by the Vaiyai's new flood (வையை வரு புனல் ஆடத் தவிர்ந்தேன்); Paripadal thirattu 2.36-39 has the rival excuse the lover's garland in her hair by the same flood (தானே புறன் தந்து வேய்தந்தது ... அறிந்து புனல் புணர்த்தது).
links.teaches: Held together, the two show that the festival flood was the stock excuse of the whole triangle: the man pleads it to his wife, and the other woman pleads it to the wife too, so the wife's scorn in the Kalittokai answers an alibi that every party in the Vaiyai festival could use.

links.note: Paripadal 6.44-51 has the learned brahmins dismayed that the flood is changed by flowers, roots, the food of common people and spilled toddy; thirattu 2.58-63 splits the refusal among பார்ப்பார், அந்தணர் and ஐயர, each for its own stain: toddy, lovers' wedding scents, honey.
links.teaches: The two songs together show that the priests' refusal to bathe was a set piece of the Vaiyai festival song, and the fragment's three causes make plain what song 6 only lists: every stain that bars the priest is a mark of the festival the town is enjoying, so the scene sets ritual purity against the river's festive use.

links.note: Akananuru 296 says the man's bathing in the great Vaiyai with the dark girl has become gossip in Koodal (அலர்ஆ கின்று, அது பலர்வாய்ப் பட்டே); thirattu 2.51-56 shows a woman wearing a garland from the flood openly, for the land to know (நாடு அறியப் பூ மாலை அப்பி), and the town's gossip following (ஊர்த்து அலர்).
links.teaches: The fragment shows how the gossip the Akananuru friend throws at the man was made: a love token worn in plain sight at the river festival, chosen by the woman as display, so the akam reproach of public shame rests on a festival custom in which the other woman wanted to be seen.

links.note: Paripadal 10.125-127 likens the flood pouring gold on the fields to the Vazhuthi pouring gold into poets' hands; thirattu 2.95-101 likens Maran bathing in the same flood with the people of Koodal to Indra bathing in the river of the sky.
links.teaches: Read together, the two Vaiyai songs place the Pandya on both sides of the flood: song 10 makes the river like the king in giving, the fragment makes the king like a god in bathing, so the king stands between the river's bounty below and Indra's heaven above, and the festival praises him through both.

new_concepts.gloss: water-play in the river or pool, especially the festival bathing of the town and of lovers in the new flood
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's words (Paripadal thirattu 2, line 97: வரு புனல் ஆடிய)

source_issues: Thirattu 2 line 4 reads சுடுகின்றே, which gives no sense in context; சூடுகின்றே (wears, crowns) is likely.
Thirattu 2 line 11 கண்னியர் and line 100 கன்ணினான் show ன for ண (கண்ணியர், கண்ணினான்); kept as written.
Thirattu 2 line 41 கயத் தகக is corrupt (perhaps கயத்துத் தக்க); line 84 மழுபொடு cannot be construed.

Thirattu 2: the core text has 101 lines but the source numbers its last line 96, and printed line 65 stands on line 67 (flags); the short half-lines 65, 67, 69 and 71 are probably the unnumbered ones.
Thirattu 2: the builder dropped lines it took for modern headings at positions 5 and 65 (flags); not checked against a second edition.
Thirattu 2 lines 29, 72 and 73 are not in sangamtamil.com's text (flag); ours kept.
Thirattu 2: the colophon has no thinai, thurai, poet or pan; the fragment survives without its frame.
